raw_case_text:
A 35-year-old blacksmith presented at the emergency department with a 3-week history of fever to 38.8 C, chills, weakness, and night sweats. The patient denied the existence of shortness of breath, chest pain, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, dysuria, and any other symptoms. His previous medical history was clear, and he mentioned no use of cigarettes, alcohol, unprocessed dairy products, or intravenous drugs. In the past, he had dental implants, and his last visit at the dentist was 6 months ago. He lives in a village, where he takes care of some chickens, rabbits, and lambs. Also, one week prior to his hospital admission, he visited his family doctor who suggested the administration of levofloxacin (500 mg/d per os) for ten days.
On admission, he was in a good level of consciousness with blood pressure of 150/76 mmHg, atmospheric air oxygen saturation of 99%, and heart rate at 93 beats/min. On clinical examination, a diastolic murmur was audible at the second right intercostal space (aortic valve area). No pathologic findings were found on lung and abdominal examination. No other mucocutaneous signs of endocarditis were observed.
Blood tests showed CRP of 2.5 mg/dl, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 20 mm/h, and white blood cell (WBC) count of 12.000/muL. Urine analysis and urine culture were negative. The chest X-ray, the electrocardiography, and the ultrasound of the abdomen were normal. Two sets (aerobic and anaerobic) of blood cultures were obtained with a difference of 20 minutes between them, and a total of 4 sets of blood cultures were finally received. The patient was initially treated with intravenous levofloxacin 500 mg and ceftriaxone 2 g per day. The serum immunological investigation for HIV, HAV, HBV, HCV, CMV, Toxoplasma, EBV, HSV, Coxsackie, RF, C3, C4, ANA, ANCA, Coxiella burnetii, Leishmania, Leptospira, and Brucella was found to be negative. The ophthalmologic examination with fundoscopy had no findings. Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography showed left ventricle dilation (ejection fraction 65%) and a degenerated bicuspid aortic valve with a small vegetation (0.5 x 0.6 cm) at the left cusp and a moderate-to-severe regurgitation. These findings are well depicted in Figures 1 and 2. Two blood cultures defined the underlying pathogen, which was Lactococcus lactis, all in anaerobic bottles. The isolate was sensitive to ampicillin, ceftriaxone, clindamycin, chloramphenicol, erythromycin, oxacillin, teicoplanin, and vancomycin. An alternative antimicrobial therapy with ceftriaxone 2 g q.d. and gentamicin 80 mg t.i.d. was initiated. During the following days, the inflammation markers dropped (CRP: 0.55 and WBC 7.53 x 103/muL), and from the fourth day of antibiotic treatment, the patient was afebrile. Two sets of blood cultures were obtained whose results were negative. On hospital day 10, administration of gentamicin was ended, and a 6-week course of intravenous ceftriaxone was given. A new transthoracic echocardiography revealed a further decrease in vegetation size. In 3 months of follow-up, the patient was symptom-free.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 35-year-old male blacksmith presented with a 3-week history of fever up to 38.8 C, chills, weakness, and night sweats.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced 3 weeks of fevers (up to 38.8 C), chills, weakness, and night sweats that persisted despite 7 days of outpatient oral levofloxacin (500 mg/day) prescribed by his family physician.
subjective.past_medical_history: Unremarkable medical history; history of dental implants with last dental visit 6 months prior; lived in a rural village and cared for chickens, rabbits, and lambs; denied smoking, alcohol, unpasteurized dairy intake, or IV drug use.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, chills, weakness, and night sweats; negative for dyspnea, chest pain, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, or dysuria.

objective.physical_examination: Alert and oriented; BP 150/76 mmHg, HR 93 bpm, SpO2 99% on room air; cardiac auscultation revealed a diastolic murmur at the right second intercostal space (aortic area); lung, abdominal, fundoscopic, and mucocutaneous examinations were normal without peripheral stigmata of endocarditis.
objective.routine_investigations: Labs showed WBC 12,000/uL, CRP 2.5 mg/dL, and ESR 20 mm/h; urinalysis, urine culture, chest X-ray, ECG, and abdominal ultrasound were normal. Serologies and immunological tests for Leishmania, Coxiella burnetii, Leptospira, Brucella, HIV, HAV, HBV, HCV, CMV, Toxoplasma, EBV, HSV, Coxsackie, RF, C3, C4, ANA, and ANCA were all negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography demonstrated left ventricular dilation (EF 65%) and a degenerated bicuspid aortic valve with a 0.5 x 0.6 cm vegetation on the left coronary cusp and moderate-to-severe aortic regurgitation. Two of four blood culture sets grew Lactococcus lactis in the anaerobic bottles (sensitive to ampicillin, ceftriaxone, clindamycin, chloramphenicol, erythromycin, oxacillin, teicoplanin, and vancomycin).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Zoonotic causes of fever of unknown origin (brucellosis, Q fever, leptospirosis, and visceral leishmaniasis) were excluded; transesophageal echocardiography and blood cultures confirmed native bicuspid aortic valve infective endocarditis caused by Lactococcus lactis. Targeted intravenous antimicrobial therapy with ceftriaxone (2 g once daily for 6 weeks) plus gentamicin (80 mg three times daily for the first 10 days) achieved defervescence by day 4, normalization of WBC and CRP, negative follow-up blood cultures, vegetation regression on repeat TTE, and symptom-free survival at 3-month follow-up.
